{{Short description|Type of stochastic process}}
'''Jump diffusion''' is a [[stochastic process]] that involves [[jump process|jumps]] and [[diffusion process|diffusion]]. It is a type of [[Lévy process]]. It has important applications in [[magnetic reconnection]], [[coronal mass ejection]]s, [[condensed matter physics]], and [[pattern theory]] and [[computational vision]].

== In physics ==

In crystals, [[atomic diffusion]] typically consists of jumps between vacant lattice sites. On time and length scales that average over many single jumps, the net motion of the jumping atoms can be described as regular [[diffusion]].

Jump diffusion can be studied on a microscopic scale by [[inelastic neutron scattering]] and by [[Mößbauer spectroscopy]]. Closed expressions for the [[autocorrelation function]] have been derived for several jump(-diffusion) models:
* Singwi, Sjölander 1960:<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Singwi | first1 = K. | last2 = Sjölander | first2 = A. | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.120.1093 | title = Resonance Absorption of Nuclear Gamma Rays and the Dynamics of Atomic Motions | journal = Physical Review | volume = 120 | issue = 4 | pages = 1093 | year = 1960 }}</ref> alternation between oscillatory motion and directed motion
* Chudley, Elliott 1961:<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Chudley | first1 = C. T. | last2 = Elliott | first2 = R. J. | doi = 10.1088/0370-1328/77/2/319 | title = Neutron Scattering from a Liquid on a Jump Diffusion Model | journal = Proceedings of the Physical Society | volume = 77 | issue = 2 | pages = 353 | year = 1961 }}</ref> jumps on a lattice
* Sears 1966,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Sears | first1 = V. F. | title = Theory of Cold Neutron Scattering by Homonuclear Diatomic Liquids: I. Free Rotation | doi = 10.1139/p66-108 | journal = Canadian Journal of Physics | volume = 44 | issue = 6 | pages = 1279–1297 | year = 1966 }}</ref> 1967:<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Sears | first1 = V. F. | title = Cold Neutron Scattering by Molecular Liquids: Iii. Methane | doi = 10.1139/p67-025 | journal = Canadian Journal of Physics | volume = 45 | issue = 2 | pages = 237–254 | year = 1967 }}</ref> jump diffusion of rotational degrees of freedom
* Hall, Ross 1981:<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Hall | first1 = P. L. | last2 = Ross | first2 = D. K. | doi = 10.1080/00268978100100521 | title = Incoherent neutron scattering functions for random jump diffusion in bounded and infinite media | journal = Molecular Physics | volume = 42 | issue = 3 | pages = 673 | year = 1981 }}</ref>  jump diffusion within a restricted volume

== In economics and finance ==
A jump-diffusion model is a form of [[mixture model]], mixing a [[jump process]] and a [[diffusion process]]. In finance, jump-diffusion models were first introduced by [[Robert C. Merton]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Merton | first1 = R. C. | author-link1 = Robert C. Merton| doi = 10.1016/0304-405X(76)90022-2 | title = Option pricing when underlying stock returns are discontinuous | journal = [[Journal of Financial Economics]]| volume = 3 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 125–144 | year = 1976 | hdl = 1721.1/1899| hdl-access = free }}</ref> Such models have a range of financial applications from [[option pricing]], to [[credit risk]], to [[time series]]  [[forecasting]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Christensen | first1 = H. L. | author-link1 = Hugh Christensen| doi = 10.1109/JSTSP.2012.2191532 | title = Forecasting high-frequency futures returns using online Langevin dynamics | journal = [[IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing]]| volume = 6 | issue = 4 | pages = 366-380 | year = 2012 | hdl = 10.1109/JSTSP.2012.2191532| hdl-access = free }}</ref> 

== In pattern theory, computer vision, and medical imaging ==
In [[pattern theory]] and [[computational vision]] in [[medical imaging]], jump-diffusion processes were first introduced by Grenander and Miller<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Grenander|first1=U.|last2=Miller|first2=M.I.|title=Representations of Knowledge in Complex Systems|journal=Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B|date=1994|volume=56|issue=4|pages=549–603|jstor=2346184}}</ref>
as a form of [[random sampling]] algorithm that mixes "focus"-like motions, the [[diffusion process]]es, with [[saccade]]-like motions, via [[jump process]]es.
The approach modelled sciences of electron-micrographs as containing multiple shapes, each having some fixed dimensional representation, with the collection of micrographs filling out the sample space corresponding to the unions of multiple finite-dimensional spaces. 
Using techniques from [[pattern theory]], a posterior probability model was constructed over the countable union of sample space; this is therefore a [[Hybrid system | hybrid system model]], containing the discrete notions of object number along with the continuum notions of shape.
The jump-diffusion process was constructed to have [[ergodic]] properties so that after initially flowing away from its initial condition it would generate samples from the posterior probability model.
